topics.title: Number and Algebra
topics.html:
Topic 1: Number and Algebra

1.10 Counting principles and the binomial theorem for rational indices

Combinations

{}^n\mathrm{C}_r=\frac{n!}{r!(n-r)!}

Permutations

{}^n\mathrm{P}_r=\frac{n!}{(n-r)!}

Binomial theorem for rational indices

(a+b)^n=a^n\left(1+\frac{b}{a}\right)^n,\quad n\in\mathbb{Q}
  • Counting principles: the multiplication and addition rules.
  • Permutations and combinations of distinct objects; arrangements of identical objects and circular arrangements are not required.
  • The expansion is an infinite series, valid for \left|\frac{b}{a}\right|<1, and is used for approximations.
  • Proof of the binomial theorem is not required.

1.11 Partial fractions

  • Splitting a rational expression into partial fractions.
  • The denominator has at most two distinct linear factors, and the degree of the numerator is less than the degree of the denominator.
  • Repeated factors, irreducible quadratic factors and improper fractions are not required.
  • Used to rearrange integrands (see 5.15).

1.12 Complex numbers in Cartesian form and the complex plane

Cartesian form

z=a+b\mathrm{i},\quad \mathrm{i}^2=-1
  • Real part, imaginary part, conjugate, modulus and argument.
  • Sums, differences, products and quotients in Cartesian form.
  • The complex plane (Argand diagram): complex numbers as points or vectors.

1.13 Modulus-argument and Euler forms of complex numbers

Modulus-argument (polar) and exponential (Euler) forms

z=r(\cos\theta+\mathrm{i}\sin\theta)=r\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta}=r\operatorname{cis}\theta
  • Conversion between Cartesian, modulus-argument and Euler forms.
  • Sums, products and quotients in any of the forms.
  • Geometric interpretation: multiplying multiplies the moduli and adds the arguments (an enlargement and a rotation).

1.14 Conjugate roots, De Moivre's theorem, powers and roots of complex numbers

De Moivre's theorem

\begin{aligned}{[r(\cos\theta+\mathrm{i}\sin\theta)]}^n&=r^n(\cos n\theta+\mathrm{i}\sin n\theta)\\&=r^n\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}n\theta}=r^n\operatorname{cis}n\theta\end{aligned}
  • Non-real roots of polynomial equations with real coefficients occur in conjugate pairs.
  • Proof of De Moivre's theorem by induction for n\in\mathbb{Z}^+; extension to rational exponents.
  • Powers and nth roots of complex numbers, including roots of unity.

1.15 Proof by induction, by contradiction and by counterexample

  • Proof by mathematical induction, for example sums of series, divisibility, derivatives and complex numbers.
  • Proof by contradiction, for example irrationality results and the infinitude of primes.
  • Disproof by a counterexample, showing why the example breaks the statement.

1.16 Systems of linear equations in up to three unknowns

  • Systems of up to three linear equations in up to three unknowns.
  • Algebraic methods (elimination or row reduction) and technology.
  • Unique solution, infinitely many solutions (general solution in terms of a parameter) or no solution (inconsistent system).
  • Links to the intersections of planes (see 3.18).

topics.title: Functions
topics.html:
Topic 2: Functions

2.12 Polynomial functions: factor and remainder theorems, sum and product of roots

Polynomial equation

\sum_{r=0}^{n}a_rx^r=0

Sum of the roots

-\frac{a_{n-1}}{a_n}

Product of the roots

\frac{(-1)^na_0}{a_n}
  • Polynomial functions: graphs, zeros, roots and factors.
  • The factor and remainder theorems.
  • Sum and product of the roots, including equations with complex roots.

2.13 Rational functions with a quadratic numerator or denominator

Linear numerator, quadratic denominator

f(x)=\frac{ax+b}{cx^2+dx+e}

Quadratic numerator, linear denominator

f(x)=\frac{ax^2+bx+c}{dx+e}
  • The reciprocal function is a special case.
  • Sketches show every asymptote (vertical, horizontal and oblique) and all intercepts with the axes.

2.14 Odd and even functions, inverses with a restricted domain, self-inverse functions

Odd function

f(-x)=-f(x)

Even function

f(-x)=f(x)

Self-inverse function

f^{-1}(x)=f(x)
  • Includes periodic functions such as \sin, \cos and \tan.
  • Finding the inverse function, restricting the domain where needed so that the inverse exists.

2.15 Solving inequalities g(x) ≥ f(x) graphically and analytically

  • Solving inequalities of the form g(x)\ge f(x), graphically and analytically.
  • Algebraic or graphical methods for simple polynomials up to degree 3.
  • Technology for these and for other functions.

2.16 Graphs of |f(x)|, f(|x|), 1/f(x), f(ax + b) and [f(x)]²; modulus equations and inequalities

Graphs drawn from the graph of y=f(x)

y=|f(x)|,\quad y=f(|x|)
y=\frac{1}{f(x)}
y=f(ax+b)
y=[f(x)]^2
  • Solving modulus equations and inequalities.
  • Algebraic methods for simple cases; technology otherwise.

topics.title: Geometry and Trigonometry
topics.html:
Topic 3: Geometry and Trigonometry

3.9 Reciprocal trigonometric ratios, Pythagorean identities and inverse trigonometric functions

Reciprocal trigonometric identities

\sec\theta=\frac{1}{\cos\theta}
\operatorname{cosec}\theta=\frac{1}{\sin\theta}
\cot\theta=\frac{1}{\tan\theta}

Pythagorean identities

1+\tan^2\theta=\sec^2\theta
1+\cot^2\theta=\operatorname{cosec}^2\theta
  • The inverse functions \arcsin x, \arccos x and \arctan x: their domains, ranges (principal values) and graphs.

3.10 Compound angle identities

Compound angle identities

\sin(A\pm B)=\sin A\cos B\pm\cos A\sin B
\cos(A\pm B)=\cos A\cos B\mp\sin A\sin B
\tan(A\pm B)=\frac{\tan A\pm\tan B}{1\mp\tan A\tan B}

Double angle identity for tan

\tan 2\theta=\frac{2\tan\theta}{1-\tan^2\theta}
  • Deriving the double angle identities from the compound angle identities.
  • Link to De Moivre's theorem.

3.11 Relationships between trigonometric functions and the symmetry of their graphs

\sin(\pi-\theta)=\sin\theta
\cos(\pi-\theta)=-\cos\theta
\tan(\pi-\theta)=-\tan\theta
  • Relationships between the trigonometric functions, seen from the symmetries of their graphs and of the unit circle.
  • Links to odd and even functions and to compound angles.

3.12 Vectors: concepts, components and algebra

Magnitude of a vector

|\boldsymbol{v}|=\sqrt{v_1^2+v_2^2+v_3^2},\quad \boldsymbol{v}=\begin{pmatrix}v_1\\v_2\\v_3\end{pmatrix}

Displacement vector

\overrightarrow{AB}=\boldsymbol{b}-\boldsymbol{a}
  • Vectors as directed line segments, in column form or with the base vectors \boldsymbol{i}, \boldsymbol{j}, \boldsymbol{k}.
  • Sums, differences, scalar multiples, the zero vector and parallel vectors, algebraically and geometrically.
  • Position vectors, unit vectors and the distance between two points.
  • Proofs of geometric properties using vectors.

3.13 The scalar product and the angle between vectors

Scalar product

\boldsymbol{v}\cdot\boldsymbol{w}=v_1w_1+v_2w_2+v_3w_3
\boldsymbol{v}\cdot\boldsymbol{w}=|\boldsymbol{v}||\boldsymbol{w}|\cos\theta

Angle between two vectors

\cos\theta=\frac{v_1w_1+v_2w_2+v_3w_3}{|\boldsymbol{v}||\boldsymbol{w}|}
  • \theta is the angle between \boldsymbol{v} and \boldsymbol{w}.
  • Perpendicular vectors: \boldsymbol{v}\cdot\boldsymbol{w}=0.
  • Parallel vectors: |\boldsymbol{v}\cdot\boldsymbol{w}|=|\boldsymbol{v}||\boldsymbol{w}|.
  • Algebraic properties of the scalar product.

3.14 Vector equation of a line in two and three dimensions

Vector equation of a line

\boldsymbol{r}=\boldsymbol{a}+\lambda\boldsymbol{b}

Parametric form

x=x_0+\lambda l,\quad y=y_0+\lambda m,\quad z=z_0+\lambda n

Cartesian equations

\frac{x-x_0}{l}=\frac{y-y_0}{m}=\frac{z-z_0}{n}
  • \boldsymbol{a} is the position vector of a point on the line and \boldsymbol{b} a direction vector.
  • Angle between two lines, from their direction vectors.
  • Simple kinematics: \lambda as time, \boldsymbol{b} as velocity and |\boldsymbol{b}| as speed.

3.15 Coincident, parallel, intersecting and skew lines

  • Coincident, parallel, intersecting and skew lines.
  • Skew lines are non-parallel and non-intersecting, which is possible only in three dimensions.
  • Finding the point of intersection of two lines.

3.16 The vector product

Vector product

\boldsymbol{v}\times\boldsymbol{w}=\begin{pmatrix}v_2w_3-v_3w_2\\v_3w_1-v_1w_3\\v_1w_2-v_2w_1\end{pmatrix}
|\boldsymbol{v}\times\boldsymbol{w}|=|\boldsymbol{v}||\boldsymbol{w}|\sin\theta

Area of a parallelogram

A=|\boldsymbol{v}\times\boldsymbol{w}|
  • \theta is the angle between \boldsymbol{v} and \boldsymbol{w}, which form two adjacent sides of the parallelogram.
  • \boldsymbol{v}\times\boldsymbol{w}=|\boldsymbol{v}||\boldsymbol{w}|\sin\theta\,\boldsymbol{n}, with the unit normal \boldsymbol{n} given by the right-hand rule.
  • Properties: anticommutative, distributive, \boldsymbol{v}\times\boldsymbol{v}=\boldsymbol{0}; for non-zero vectors the product is zero exactly when they are parallel.
  • Area of a triangle.

3.17 Vector and Cartesian equations of a plane

Vector equation of a plane

\boldsymbol{r}=\boldsymbol{a}+\lambda\boldsymbol{b}+\mu\boldsymbol{c}

Equation of a plane using the normal vector

\boldsymbol{r}\cdot\boldsymbol{n}=\boldsymbol{a}\cdot\boldsymbol{n}

Cartesian equation of a plane

ax+by+cz=d
  • \boldsymbol{b} and \boldsymbol{c} are non-parallel vectors in the plane; \boldsymbol{n} is a normal to the plane.

3.18 Intersections and angles between lines and planes

  • Intersection of a line with a plane, of two planes and of three planes.
  • Found by solving equations and interpreted geometrically: a point, a line, a plane or no intersection.
  • Links to systems of linear equations (see 1.16).
  • Angle between a line and a plane, and between two planes.

topics.title: Statistics and Probability
topics.html:
Topic 4: Statistics and Probability

4.13 Bayes' theorem

Bayes' theorem

\mathrm{P}(B\mid A)=\frac{\mathrm{P}(B)\,\mathrm{P}(A\mid B)}{\mathrm{P}(B)\,\mathrm{P}(A\mid B)+\mathrm{P}(B')\,\mathrm{P}(A\mid B')}

With three events

\mathrm{P}(B_i\mid A)=\frac{\mathrm{P}(B_i)\,\mathrm{P}(A\mid B_i)}{\begin{gathered}\mathrm{P}(B_1)\mathrm{P}(A\mid B_1)+\mathrm{P}(B_2)\mathrm{P}(A\mid B_2)\\{}+\mathrm{P}(B_3)\mathrm{P}(A\mid B_3)\end{gathered}}
  • Reversing a conditional probability, for example updating the chance of a disease from a test result.
  • At most three events in the partition.

4.14 Discrete and continuous random variables: pdfs, mean, variance, median and mode

Variance

\mathrm{Var}(X)=\mathrm{E}\bigl((X-\mu)^2\bigr)=\mathrm{E}(X^2)-[\mathrm{E}(X)]^2

Discrete random variable

\begin{aligned}\mathrm{Var}(X)&=\sum (x-\mu)^2\,\mathrm{P}(X=x)\\&=\sum x^2\,\mathrm{P}(X=x)-\mu^2\end{aligned}

Continuous random variable

\mathrm{E}(X)=\mu=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}x\,f(x)\,\mathrm{d}x
\begin{aligned}\mathrm{Var}(X)&=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}(x-\mu)^2f(x)\,\mathrm{d}x\\&=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}x^2f(x)\,\mathrm{d}x-\mu^2\end{aligned}

Linear transformation of a single random variable

\mathrm{E}(aX+b)=a\mathrm{E}(X)+b
\mathrm{Var}(aX+b)=a^2\,\mathrm{Var}(X)
  • Probability density functions, including piecewise functions; the total area under the curve is 1.
  • Mode and median of a continuous random variable.
  • Standard deviation, and fair games.

topics.title: Calculus
topics.html:
Topic 5: Calculus

5.12 Continuity, differentiability, limits and differentiation from first principles

Derivative from first principles

f'(x)=\lim_{h\to 0}\frac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h}
  • Informal understanding of continuity and differentiability at a point.
  • Limits: convergence and divergence.
  • First principles is used for polynomials only.
  • Higher derivatives, with the notations \frac{\mathrm{d}^ny}{\mathrm{d}x^n} and f^{(n)}(x), including patterns proved by induction.

5.13 Limits by l'Hôpital's rule or Maclaurin series

Standard limit

\lim_{\theta\to 0}\frac{\sin\theta}{\theta}=1
  • Limits of \frac{f(x)}{g(x)} as x\to a or x\to\infty that give the indeterminate forms \frac{0}{0} or \frac{\infty}{\infty}.
  • Found with l'Hôpital's rule, repeated if needed, or with Maclaurin series.
  • Links to horizontal asymptotes.

5.14 Implicit differentiation, related rates of change and optimisation

  • Implicit differentiation of relations in x and y.
  • Related rates of change, linked by the chain rule.
  • Optimisation problems, including a greatest or least value at an endpoint of the domain.

5.15 Further standard derivatives and integrals

Standard derivatives

\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}(\tan x)=\sec^2x
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}(\sec x)=\sec x\tan x
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}(\operatorname{cosec}x)=-\operatorname{cosec}x\cot x
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}(\cot x)=-\operatorname{cosec}^2x
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}(a^x)=a^x\ln a
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}(\log_a x)=\frac{1}{x\ln a}
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}(\arcsin x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}(\arccos x)=-\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}(\arctan x)=\frac{1}{1+x^2}

Standard integrals

\int a^x\,\mathrm{d}x=\frac{1}{\ln a}a^x+C
\int \frac{1}{a^2+x^2}\,\mathrm{d}x=\frac{1}{a}\arctan\left(\frac{x}{a}\right)+C
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{a^2-x^2}}\,\mathrm{d}x=\arcsin\left(\frac{x}{a}\right)+C,\quad |x|<a
  • Indefinite integrals of the derivatives above, and composites of these with a linear function.
  • Partial fractions (up to two distinct linear factors) are used to rearrange integrands.

5.16 Integration by substitution and by parts

Integration by parts

\int u\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}\,\mathrm{d}x=uv-\int v\frac{\mathrm{d}u}{\mathrm{d}x}\,\mathrm{d}x

or

\int u\,\mathrm{d}v=uv-\int v\,\mathrm{d}u
  • Integration by substitution: the substitution is given unless the integral has the form \int k\,g'(x)\,f(g(x))\,\mathrm{d}x.
  • Limits change with the substitution in definite integrals.
  • Repeated integration by parts, including cyclic cases such as \int \mathrm{e}^x\sin x\,\mathrm{d}x.

5.17 Areas against the y-axis and volumes of revolution

Area of a region enclosed by a curve and the y-axis

A=\int_a^b x\,\mathrm{d}y

Volume of revolution about the x-axis or y-axis

V=\int_a^b \pi y^2\,\mathrm{d}x \quad\text{or}\quad V=\int_a^b \pi x^2\,\mathrm{d}y
  • Rotation through 2\pi about the axis.
  • Includes regions between two curves.

5.18 First-order differential equations

Euler's method

y_{n+1}=y_n+h\times f(x_n,y_n),\quad x_{n+1}=x_n+h

Integrating factor for y'+P(x)y=Q(x)

\mathrm{e}^{\int P(x)\,\mathrm{d}x}

Homogeneous equation

\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}=f\left(\frac{y}{x}\right),\quad\text{using the substitution } y=vx
  • Numerical solution of \frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}=f(x,y) by Euler's method, where h is a constant (the step length).
  • Separation of variables, including the logistic equation with partial fractions.
  • Contexts include cooling, population growth and radioactive decay.

5.19 Maclaurin series

Maclaurin series

f(x)=f(0)+xf'(0)+\frac{x^2}{2!}f''(0)+\dots

Maclaurin series for special functions

\mathrm{e}^x=1+x+\frac{x^2}{2!}+\dots
\ln(1+x)=x-\frac{x^2}{2}+\frac{x^3}{3}-\dots
\sin x=x-\frac{x^3}{3!}+\frac{x^5}{5!}-\dots
\cos x=1-\frac{x^2}{2!}+\frac{x^4}{4!}-\dots
\arctan x=x-\frac{x^3}{3}+\frac{x^5}{5}-\dots
  • Series for (1+x)^p with p\in\mathbb{Q}.
  • New series by substitution, products, differentiation and integration.
  • Series developed from a differential equation by repeated differentiation.
